summary: This informational document defines a methodology for measuring how long a network forwarding device takes to resume forwarding after a reset. It covers different reset types, such as software and hardware restarts. The aim is to make results from different devices comparable for benchmarking.

eli5.summary: When a computer reboots, you wonder how long until it works again. This document is a stopwatch recipe for routers, so everyone times a restart the same way.

subtitle: A standard way to time how long a router or switch is out of action after a restart.

tldr.problem: Forwarding devices get restarted, and forwarding may stop meanwhile, but modern hardware and software features make the recovery time hard to compare between devices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines reset time and two ways to measure it, frame loss or timestamps, then gives test procedures for hardware resets, software resets and power interruption.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2544 and, only for the term reset time, RFC 1242, so reset results are reported consistently.

facts.label: Power interruption length
facts.value: At least 15 seconds (subtracted from the result)

today: RFC 6201 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 1242 and RFC 2544. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Scope and Reset Time
sections.content:
A reset is any restart of a forwarding device or one of its components. Forwarding may be interrupted during it, so it is useful to know how long the device takes to resume. Features like distributed forwarding and graceful restart make the answer less simple than it used to be.

Reset time is defined as the total time a device is out of operation, including the time to perform the reset and the time to recover from it. It is measured in milliseconds. The document updates Section 26.6 of RFC 2544 and defines the term, updating RFC 1242. Software upgrades and RIB and FIB scaling are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Reset time is how long a machine is out of action, from the moment it is switched off until it is fully working again.

sections.title: How Reset Time Is Measured
sections.content:
There are two accepted methods. In the frame-loss method, the tester knows the offered rate in packets per second and divides the number of frames lost by that rate. In the timestamp method, the tester timestamps each frame, records the timestamp of the last frame received before the interruption (A) and the first frame after it (B), and the difference B minus A is the reset time.

The operator MAY use either, depending on the test tool. Frame loss SHOULD be used if the tool can count lost frames per stream and keeps transmitting regardless of link status. The timestamp method SHOULD be used if the tool can timestamp every frame and transmits only while the link is up. If both are possible, use the more accurate one.
sections.eli5: You either count how many messages got lost and work out the time from that, or you note when the last message arrived before the outage and the first one after, and subtract.

sections.title: Test Requirements and Reporting
sections.content:
Tests SHOULD first be run with forwarding state that does not depend on outside sources, such as static routing and address resolution, and MAY then be repeated with dynamic protocols. The tester MUST use identical control and data plane information across devices, and document factors that can affect reset time, such as the type of reset, manual or automatic, scheduled or not, local or remote, and scale (line cards, interfaces, routing protocol instances, routing table entries, route processors).

Results are reported as frame loss, if measured, and reset time. The RECOMMENDED parameters include throughput, average loss in frames, average reset time in milliseconds, the number of trials, protocol, frame size, port media, port speed and interface encapsulation. Multiple trials and averaged results are RECOMMENDED. If the reset time is zero, only "no loss" is reported.
sections.eli5: To compare fairly, every machine gets the same test, and you write down everything that could change the answer, like how big the machine is.

sections.title: The Reset Tests
sections.content:
Three kinds of reset are covered. A hardware reset re-initializes one or more physical components, such as the Routing Processor or a line card. A software reset re-initializes only software state, for example an operating system or a single process. A power interruption is the complete loss of power, which re-initializes all hardware and software. Each test is marked REQUIRED or OPTIONAL.

Every procedure follows the same pattern: save the configuration and boot parameters, confirm the device forwards traffic for at least 15 seconds using minimum-size frames at a rate that reaches maximum throughput, trigger the reset, then record frame loss or timestamps and compute the reset time. Reset by CLI, switch or button is RECOMMENDED over physically removing parts. For a power interruption the outage SHOULD last at least 15 seconds, and 15 seconds are removed from the reported reset time.
sections.eli5: First check it works for a while, then restart it in one of three ways, and time how long until traffic flows again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking is limited to controlled lab tests on dedicated address space. The test network MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the management network. Testing is black-box and uses only externally observable measurements.

Devices SHOULD NOT have special capabilities just for benchmarking, and any security implications SHOULD be the same in the lab and in production. The RFC states there are no specific security considerations in its scope.
sections.eli5: Do the testing in a closed lab so test traffic cannot leak into real networks.
